summary:
Malawi is dangerous for trans visitors. On 28 June 2024 a three-member panel of the Constitutional Court rejected the challenge to Penal Code sections 153, 154 and 156, which carry up to fourteen years' imprisonment, and left any reform to parliament. Human Rights Watch called the decision a dark day and warned of heightened risks of arbitrary arrest and violence against LGBT people.

The application was brought by Dutch national Jan Willen Akster and Jana Gonani, a trans woman who had received an eight-year sentence in a men's prison in December 2021. Faith-based groups filed briefs in the proceedings, and religious leaders led nationwide protests claiming that the case sought to legalise same-sex marriage.

Human Rights Watch reported in October 2018, in the 61-page report 'Let Posterity Judge' based on interviews with 45 LGBT people in Lilongwe and Blantyre alongside lawyers, activists and officials, that police arbitrarily arrested and detained transgender people, sometimes assaulting them, and that medical staff denied services on gender-expression grounds: a trans man was beaten and then refused treatment, and nurses mocked people presenting for HIV tests. The report found that people whose gender expression differs from expectations are most likely to be targeted.

Sections 153 and 156 carry up to 14 years for men and five years for women. A 2012 justice-minister moratorium on arrests was reaffirmed in December 2015 but suspended by the Mzuzu High Court in 2016 after religious leaders' litigation, leaving its legality contested; in April 2018 police in Mzuzu charged Limbani Sibande under section 156 rather than section 153, apparently to circumvent the moratorium while both laws faced constitutional challenge.

Arrests carry severe community consequences. In December 2015 two men arrested on homosexuality charges suffered house ransacking, assault by neighbours, threats of being burned alive, attempted extortion, forced stripping, forced medical and HIV/STD examinations by community police, and distribution of their photos on social media.

There is no legal process for gender recognition in Malawi. The Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Law, in force from 17 April 2015, bans all same-sex marriages and states that gender is assigned at birth, barring marriage between a person who has undergone gender reassignment surgery and someone of that person's prior gender. No broad legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity exist; since 2019 limited protection exists only against hate speech through the Communications (Broadcasting) Regulations 2019, which bar broadcast content likely to incite hatred on account of gender identity or sexual preference.

State hostility is documented at the highest levels. In April 2010 President Bingu wa Mutharika called same-sex marriage evil, and in July 2011 he threatened activists Undule Mwakasungula and Gift Trapence, saying he would hunt them in their homes and smoke them out, forcing them into hiding amid treason threats. The 2011 U.S. State Department report found senior officials created a discriminatory environment and documented the July 2011 protest killings that left 20 dead. In January 2016 People's Party spokesperson Ken Msonda posted that gays are worse than dogs and should be killed; the Malawi Law Society filed charges, but the director of public prosecution took over and discontinued the case on 21 January. In February 2014 the Muslim Association of Malawi called for the death penalty for gay people, and on 4 January 2017 thousands across 28 districts marched against legalising homosexuality in protests led by the Episcopal Conference of Malawi and the Evangelical Association of Malawi.

Malawi does not recognise same-sex unions. At the 2011 Universal Periodic Review the government rejected every recommendation to decriminalise same-sex relations, stating it had no plans to legalize homosexuality. The UN Human Rights Committee's June 2012 provisional concluding observations urged Malawi to amend the Penal Code and protect same-sex couples from violence; Malawi has failed to file its ICCPR report for over 17 years.

Community visibility is emerging but fragile. The country's first pride parade was held in Lilongwe on 26 June 2021, organised by the Nyasa Rainbow Alliance with over 50 attendees delivering a petition for marriage equality and healthcare access. Public hostility is documented: bail was denied to Tiwonge Chimbalanga and Monjeza in 2009 because the public was angry with them, and a January 2016 interview in which gay man Eric Sambisa said kill us or give us our rights led to his brief police detention and time in hiding.
tangentialFactors:
Malawi is described as a highly conservative country where, in the government's own 2012 UN report, the vast majority of society has not accepted homosexuality and it is not practiced in the open. Donor pressure has been contested domestically: the Malawi Council of Churches urged international organisations to refrain from using aid as a means of forcing the country to legalise homosexuality, and Justice Minister George Chaponda blamed civil society leaders for withdrawn foreign aid.

Media treatment of trans people is unreliable. International outlets failed to report trans woman Tiwonge Chimbalanga's gender identity during her trial, and in 2010 Peter Sawali was arrested and sentenced to 60 days for posting Gay rights are human rights posters in Blantyre.

Some officials have pushed for inclusion: in September 2009 Mary Shawa, secretary for nutrition, HIV and AIDS in the president's office, argued Malawi must give gay people access to HIV and AIDS services on a human rights basis, and CEDEP's Gift Trapence has contrasted arrests with government Global Fund money for LGBTI HIV services.
localsOnly:
Residents face the Penal Code sections 153, 154 and 156 with penalties up to 14 years for men and five years for women, and no legal gender recognition process exists. The 2012 moratorium on arrests remains legally contested after the Mzuzu High Court suspended it in 2016, and police have been documented charging under section 156 to circumvent it.

Discrimination protections are minimal: only the Communications (Broadcasting) Regulations 2019 provide limited cover against hate speech referencing gender identity or sexual preference, with no broad non-discrimination law on sexual orientation or gender identity.

Community organising continues despite risk. The Nyasa Rainbow Alliance's June 2021 Lilongwe pride parade drew over 50 attendees and delivered a petition to city officials demanding better healthcare access for LGBTQ people, while the 2018 Human Rights Watch report documented arbitrary arrest, physical violence and discrimination against LGBTQ community members.
outOfScopeNotes:
The current enforcement posture of the 2012 arrest moratorium after the June 2024 Constitutional Court ruling is unresolved in the sources: the court left reform to parliament, but no source confirms whether parliament has acted or whether police are currently making arrests under sections 153/154/156.

Whether the Communications (Broadcasting) Regulations 2019 hate-speech provisions have been invoked in any enforcement action is not sourced.

Malawi's compliance with the UN Human Rights Committee's 2012 concluding observations and the status of its overdue ICCPR report are noted as unresolved; no source confirms subsequent filing.

Access to gender-affirming care for visitors is not directly sourced; the 2018 findings on denial of medical services to transgender people are the closest available evidence.
